title: Memory of past lives
content_html:
Memory of past lives

In Buddhist traditions, especially Theravāda and Tibetan, advanced meditators (and the Buddha himself) are described as recalling past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa). These memories are framed not as a “soul’s journey” but as the continuity of causal streams of consciousness, conditioned by karma.

From a scientific standpoint, no empirical evidence supports literal recall of lives before birth. Neuroscience treats memory as dependent on the brain, memories are stored in distributed cortical traces. Without a functioning brain, recall as we understand it is not possible. Reports of “past life memories” are interpreted in naturalistic ways, for example, the brain fills gaps with constructed stories, forgotten memories resurface, misattributed as new), or as dream-like states during deep meditation, where symbolic imagery feels real. Cultural expectation also shapes phenomenology: traditions prime practitioners to interpret certain inner experiences as “previous lives.”

A few modern frameworks try to “translate” the concept: the brain’s capacity for vivid scene construction (hippocampus + default mode network) may allow meditators to generate lifelike experiences that feel like memory. Implicit memory / generational transmission: epigenetic or intergenerational trauma research shows that traces of past generations can shape present cognition and affect. Some compare this to “carrying” lives not directly remembered. Constructive mind model: both neuroscience and Buddhism agree that memory is reconstructive, not literal. Past-life recall may be seen as an extreme case of reconstruction shaped by cultural and ethical framing. For neuroscience, the key issue is substrate: memory requires a physical basis (neurons). Without continuity of the same brain, memory continuity across lives is unexplained. For Buddhism, continuity is causal, not material: what persists is not memory traces but a flow of conditions (karma) that can manifest as recollection in certain states.
